# Language environments of infants in the NICU improve after a brief parent education intervention

Rachel R. Romeo 1, Nikita S. Kalluri 2, Vanessa Young 3, Stephanie Heather Kinlay3, Rylee Kerper3 and Anne R. Hansen 3,4✉

© The Author(s) 2026

Infants in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) face high risk for language delays, compounded by limited parent-infant interaction. Although intensive parent programs are effective, it is unclear whether brief interventions can also promote positive outcomes. We developed a brief, 30-min language education for parents, and conducted a randomized controlled trial of 100 infants across two NICUs assigned to either receive the intervention or standard care. Parents who received the intervention showed signiﬁcantly greater pre-to-post gains in knowledge of infant cognitive and language development, and their infants experienced larger increases in speech exposure during family visits. Moderations revealed that the intervention was especially effective for parents with lower education levels, and whose infants had complex medical needs. Findings indicate that a brief educational intervention can meaningfully enhance parental knowledge and infant language exposure in the NICU. Future work should assess whether this accessible approach may reduce disparities in long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.

Journal of Perinatology; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41372-026-02739-1

INTRODUCTION Infants hospitalized in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) are at high risk for adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes, including delayed language development [1–5]. In addition to risks from infants’ underlying medical concerns, the complexity of the NICU setting itself may inﬂuence early language development due to loud and disruptive environments, or result in decreased parent-infant communication and bonding [6–10]. There is considerable research on the positive impact of frequent, high-quality language exposure for children’s linguistic, cognitive, and even neural development [11–13]. Early language interaction and communication exposure may be even more crucial for premature and/or medically complex infants. Longitudinal research shows that infants in NICUs who are exposed to increased adult speech have better cognitive and language outcomes later in childhood, long after discharge [14]. Parents are the primary source of language exposure for preterm infants, who vocalize more when their parents are speaking to them [15, 16]. Therefore, advocating for parents to provide high quality communication to their hospitalized infants may ultimately improve their neurodevelopmental and language outcomes [17, 18]. The NICU environment presents multiple barriers to intentional language exposure, including infant clinical instability, physical barriers of equipment (e.g., incubators), and time limitations of parent visits [9, 19]. To better understand NICUspeciﬁc barriers to frequent, high-quality parent-infant communication, we previously conducted a qualitative research study with clinical providers and family members [20].

A common theme identiﬁed was the lack of education for families about the importance of language exposure and approaches to increase the quality of communication. This was especially important for parents of infants with high medical complexity (e.g., intubated, sedated) who did not know whether, or how, to communicate with their babies [20]. To date, there are very few reports of evidence-based interventions to facilitate high-quality communication between parents and infants while in the NICU [21]. One recent randomized controlled trial (RCT) in a tertiary NICU reported improved speech environments and positive developmental language outcomes, the intervention involved six lessons and personalized feedback over the course of six weeks [22]. The substantial time commitment such intensive interventions require of both parents and staff limits the feasibility of widespread implementation in busy NICU environments. It remains to be established whether a shorter, “light-touch” intervention could demonstrate similar effects. Furthermore, there is a need to move beyond average intervention effects and investigate factors associated with variations in intervention efﬁcacy, such as infants’ medical complexity and parental resources. To address these gaps, we designed a brief education program for parents of infants hospitalized in the NICU aimed at promoting more frequent, high-quality language exposure. We compared randomized intervention and control groups on changes in (1) parents’ knowledge of infant linguistic and cognitive development and (2) infants’ auditory speech exposure. We examined intervention efﬁcacy across a variety of infant and family characteristics.

METHODS Participants and setting This was a prospective Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) of 100 infants, from February 2021 through April 2024, with half of participants (n = 50) assigned to the intervention and half to the control group. Based on moderate effect sizes found in a simple intervention with 6–10-month-old infants [23]. and natural development and maturational changes in the NICU [15]. For 80% power at alpha <0.05, we estimated a sample size of 50 infants in each study group. A random number generator was used to prospectively assign participants (1–100) to either the intervention or control before they were recruited. Participant enrollment was not intentionally blinded given the objectivity of outcome measures. Infants were admitted to two NICUs in Boston, Massachusetts: A Level IV referral NICU (n = 73) and a level III NICU with an associated delivery unit (n = 27). The level IV NICU had an open-bay design for the ﬁrst 40 participants before moving to a new unit with exclusively private rooms; the level III NICU had double rooms throughout. To be eligible, infants needed to have an expected NICU stay for the duration of the study (5 days), the parent needed to feel comfortable communicating in English, and the clinical team needed to approve approaching the parents for informed consent. All families received a children’s book as thanks for participating.

Procedures Study procedures were approved by the IRB of Boston Children’s Hospital. See Fig. 1 for the study timeline. A parent or legal guardian provided informed consent for participation.

Intervention curriculum The curriculum was developed by the research team and consisted of seven videos (watched on an iPad) and two handouts, all publicly available (links provided in the Supplement). The content focused on early brain development and the importance of responsive, interactive communication between infants and caregivers, with demonstrations of techniques for interacting with infants at varying development levels to promote language exposure and emotional bonding. Delivery of the curriculum lasted approximately 30 min.

Measures Demographics. We collected parent-reported demographic information including parental age, gender, education level, marital status, and parent and infant race and ethnicity. We followed the hospitals standard classiﬁcation system for race and ethnicity, namely White/Caucasian; Black/African American; Asian/Paciﬁc Islander; Other; and Multiple for race, and Hispanic vs Non-Hispanic for ethnicity. We abstracted additional demographics from the medical record including infant gestational age (GA), chronological age (CA), postmenstrual age (PMA), and plurality (i.e., singleton vs. multiple gestation). Additional measures of infant medical severity were also abstracted from the medical record. These include whether infants had any neurological or hearing concerns, were intubated, or were sedated/ chemically paralyzed during the study—all of which could affect caregivers’ tendency to speak to them. Further, the State Behavioral Scale (SBS) score [24]. is a measure used to assess an infant’s level of sedation and agitation, with extremely strong discriminant validity (F = 75.8, p < 0.001) between six possible scores: –3 (fully unresponsive), –2

(responsive to noxious stimuli), –1 (responsive to gentle touch or voice), 0 (awake and able to calm), +1 (restless and difﬁcult to calm), and +2 (agitated). Finally, the Complexity Assessment and Monitoring to Ensure Optimal Outcomes (CAMEO) [25, 26]. is a measure of acuity based on nursing cognitive workload complexity; content validity was established through a modiﬁed Delphi process with a multi-ICU expert panel. Scores range from 54 to >121, with higher scores indicating greater cognitive workload complexity, and are organized into ﬁve classiﬁcations (I–V) ranging from clinically stable patients requiring basic monitoring and care coordination to those who are clinically unstable with uncertain outcomes, requiring frequent intensive assessment, multiple interventions, and complex family support. This measure was only available for the infants in the Level IV NICU.

SPEAK survey. Parents’ knowledge of language and cognition development was measured using the infant version of the Survey of Parent/ Provider Expectations and Knowledge—Clinical tool (Baby SPEAK-C) [26]. This 10-item validated survey is designed for clinical providers to assess caregivers’ understanding and misconceptions about infants’ language and cognitive development and related caregiving practices. Parents are asked to consider 0- to 12-month-old infants and answer how true each statement is on a 4-point Likert scale. Higher scores indicate higher knowledge, with a maximum score of 30 points. The SPEAK was developed and validated through a rigorous multi-phase process including cognitive interviews, expert consultations, and multiple ﬁeld tests. Item response theory (IRT) and Rasch modeling were used to evaluate psychometric properties; the resulting instrument demonstrates strong internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.84), person-separation reliability (0.84–0.85), and concurrent validity with other measures of parenting knowledge (r = 0.24) and children’s linguistic and cognitive environments (r = 0.20–0.34) [27, 28]. Scores were logit-transformed before analysis to address negative skew.

LENA recording. Infants’ speech exposure was measured using the Language Environment Analysis (LENA) system, in which a non-intrusive digital language recorder captures full days (up to 16 h) of children’s auditory language exposure [29]. and which has been successfully used in prior NICU research [14–16, 22, 30, 31]. LENA software provides an automated estimate of the number of words spoken by adults to/near the child (“adult words”), the number of infant vocalizations (“child vocalizations”), and the number of reciprocal vocal interactions between the child and any adult (“conversational turns”). Given infants’ conditions and young ages, we focused on the number of adult words, consistent with prior NICU research [14, 15, 22, 24]. The adult word count (AWC) measure has demonstrated strong validity across studies, with a mean correlation of r = 0.79 between automated and manually transcribed word counts in a systematic review of 33 validation studies [32] and speciﬁcally in the NICU context, AWC has been shown to provide valid estimates of adult speech even in the challenging acoustic environment of neonatal care [33]. Recorders were placed next to the infant (in the incubator or crib) at approximately 7:00 am on each recording day and automatically shut off after 16 h. On days when the LENA recording occurred, family members documented their presence at the bedside using a sign-in sheet (time in, time out, person/people present). Analyses were limited to times when at least one family member was present at the bedside. Analyses We ﬁt generalized estimating equations (GEEs) predicting Time 2 outcomes (adult words per minute and SPEAK scores) from the Time 1 counterparts. All models clustered observations by family to account for sibling pairs and used an exchangeable working correlation with robust (sandwich) standard errors. Follow-up models also included additional covariates as sensitivity checks and to examine potential independent effects on outcomes. Covariates included: hospital site; participating parent’s gender, age, and education level; whether this was their ﬁrst baby; infant’s assigned sex, age (GA, CA, and PMA), SBS and CAMEO scores, intubation and chemical paralysis status, presence of neurological/auditory concerns, and Time 1–Time 2 change in total visitor minutes. Finally, group-by-covariate interaction terms were added to examine whether intervention effects varied according to any demographic or clinical measure. Analyses were conducted in R using geepack for GEEs and emmeans for estimated marginal means and contrasts. Each analysis uses listwise deletion to only examine complete cases (ﬁnal N = 93 for SPEAK analyses, N = 90 for LENA analyses). Results for the SPEAK survey are reported as odds ratios (OR) and predicted mean scores, while results for the adult words are reported as a ratio of means (Intervention/Control) with corresponding percent differences. Signiﬁcant interactions for continuous variables are described and visualized via median-splits.

RESULTS Sample Complete participant demographics (infant and parent) are reported in Table 1. Ninety-two participants completed the entire study, while 8 (4 intervention, 4 control) did not complete all measures due to discharge/transfer to another unit or change in clinical status. See Fig. 2 for a CONSORT diagram of participation/ attrition. Parents who completed the questionnaires and intervention were primarily mothers (84%), but varied widely in age, race and ethnicity, and education level. Sixty-ﬁve percent of parents reported this was their ﬁrst child. At enrollment, infants (45% female) ranged in GA from 22.4 to 40.7 weeks, CA from 2 days–42.7 weeks and PMA from 31.0 to 68.7 weeks. Diagnoses varied widely, with 38% having neurological or auditory concerns, 26% were intubated, and 4% were chemically paralyzed. Most infants (69%) had an SBS score of 0, indicating they were awake and able to calm, and CAMEO scores ranged from 71-143, corresponding to levels II-V (where V is the highest level of care complexity) (Table 1). Two families in the control group were excluded from LENA analyses for having large differences ( > 3 SD)

in the number of family visitation minutes between Time 1 and Time 2. There were no signiﬁcant differences between intervention and control groups for any infant or parent demographic measures (all p > 0.2).

Intervention effects on parents’ knowledge of infant cognitive & language development Parents whose infants were assigned to the intervention group had higher Time 2 SPEAK scores (controlling for Time 1) compared to controls (OR = 2.79, 95% CI = 1.94–4.01, p < 0.0001; Fig. 3A). Speciﬁcally, the intervention group exhibited an estimated 7.6% increase, while the control group exhibited only a 0.8% increase. This result remained signiﬁcant after controlling for all parent and infant demographic measures (all p < 0.001). There was also a signiﬁcant independent effect of recruitment site, such that parents from the level III NICU scored higher on average than the parents from the level IV NICU (OR = 1.65, 95% CI = 1.12–2.41, p = 0.01). There were also a signiﬁcant interaction between group assignment and infants’ SBS scores (OR = 2.08, 95% CI = 1.37–3.15, p < 0.001), such that the intervention was most effective at increasing parents’ SPEAK scores when infants had higher SBS scores (i.e., were more awake; Fig. 3B). Speciﬁcally, when infants were awake (SBS ≥0), the intervention led to an estimated 13.8% score increase, while when the infant was sedated or unresponsive (SBS < 0), there was only a 7.6% increase.

Intervention effects on infants’ language environments Infants of parents who were assigned to the intervention group experienced more adult words per minute at Time 2 (controlling for Time 1) compared to those in the control group (OR = 1.43, 95% CI = 1.13–1.82, p = 0.004; Fig. 4A). Speciﬁcally, the intervention group exhibited an estimated 8.4% increase, while the control group exhibited an estimated decrease of 26.6%. This result remained signiﬁcant after controlling for all parent and infant demographic measures (all p < 0.04). There were also signiﬁcant interactions between group assignment and infant intubation status (OR = 1.72, 95% CI = 0.88–3.36, p = 0.01; Fig. 4B), parents’ education level (OR = 0.88, 95% CI = 0.80–0.98, p = 0.021; Fig. 4C), and participating parent gender (OR = 0.47, 95% CI = 0.23–0.94, p = 0.032); Fig. 4D. There was also a signiﬁcant moderation by infant chemical paralysis status (OR = 1.68, 95% CI = 1.18–2.40, p = 0.004), with greater speech increases for chemically paralyzed infants; however, only n = 4 infants in the full study, and n = 1 in the intervention group were chemically paralyzed, so this ﬁnding should be interpreted with caution.

DISCUSSION In this randomized controlled trial, we found that a brief parental education program for NICU parents led to a signiﬁcant improvement in parents’ knowledge of infant cognitive and language development, as well as short term infant language exposure in the NICU, even after adjusting for sociodemographic factors known to affect language exposure. Given that infants who are hospitalized in the NICU are often at high risk of

neurocognitive delays, this intervention provides a highly feasible opportunity to maximize in-hospital language exposure and potentially improve infants’ neurodevelopment outcomes. While it was beyond the scope of this research to assess longer term outcomes, it helps lay the foundation for sustained language enrichment. Parents of infants hospitalized in the NICU are a particularly valuable target for this intervention, as it provides a practical, actionable skillset that has long-term beneﬁts for their child. In recent years, family integration in NICU care has been shown to improve parental mental health and infant health outcomes [34]. including long-term neurodevelopment. However, speciﬁc caregiving behaviors within the NICU targeting neurodevelopmental outcomes are vastly understudied. In-unit education has been shown to effectively promote several practical caregiving skills, including infant feeding, bathing, and administering medications [35, 36]. However, our prior investigation found that, given the social and medical complexity of a NICU hospitalization,

families often do not feel empowered or informed about the importance and logistics of speaking to their infants [20]. This leads these already high risk infants admitted to a NICU to have lower exposure to language and parental conversation, and therefore less auditory stimulation during a critical period of brain development. The educational intervention described in this study improved parental understanding of the importance of adult speech to infant cognition and language development, offering an accessible and targeted way for families to contribute to their infant’s development, and another method of family integration into NICU care. In older infants, the frequency of language exposure at home has been associated with improved cognition throughout childhood [37]. In the NICU, exposure to an increased number of adult words has also been shown to relate to better language development in the ﬁrst years of life [14]. Most efforts to increase infant language exposure in the NICU has been limited to playing audio-recordings of parental voices or parental reading interventions [21]. Recently, an intensive 6-week intervention for families of preterm infants in a level III NICU demonstrated increased infant language exposure in the NICU and long-term beneﬁts to children’s language development [22]. Our work builds on prior literature by demonstrating that a brief, accessible, and feasibly scalable intervention resulted in short term increased language exposure for infants in both level III and level IV NICUs—similar to that seen in prior intensive interventions—accompanied by improvements in parents’ knowledge of language and cognitive development that may inﬂuence their future, post-discharge interactions. Importantly, we also show that the intervention provided the greatest beneﬁts for the most at-risk infants, offering promising next steps toward mitigating established sociodemographic disparities in neonatal outcomes. Additionally, intervention effects on infants’ language exposure were greatest for infants who were intubated, and potentially for those who were chemically paralyzed, although this sub-sample was very small (n = 4) and ﬁndings may not be interpretable. This is consistent with ﬁndings from our prior qualitative study, in which we surveyed NICU families and providers about their views on communicating with infants in the NICU [20]. Parents noted their intimidation, lack of knowledge, and fear about communicating with acutely ill infants —especially when they were intubated and/or required other invasive equipment—often not knowing if their babies could hear them, if talking might cause more harm than good, or feeling like

they needed permission to interact and communicate. The present intervention likely provided families of acutely ill infants the conﬁdence to communicate with their infants, leading to the greatest increases in language exposure. On average, children whose parents have attained higher levels of education are exposed to more child directed speech than those whose parents had lower educational attainment, leading to higher lexical development through early childhood [38]. This effect is magniﬁed in children with high medical complexity, a risk factor for NICU graduates [39]. While the parent education level was overall high, the present intervention led to the greatest increases in infants’ language exposure when parents had lower educational attainment. This offers a concrete step toward improving equitable outcomes. This is especially notable given that other language-focused interventions in medical settings had effects limited to higher SES parents [40]. Additionally, the intervention was most effective when the father was the parent who participated. Note that this does not mean that fathers necessarily spoke more to their infants, because the LENA records all speech from all nearby adults when visitors are present, and we are unable to determine exactly who was speaking when. However, in families where the father was the participating parent, the father also spent more time at the bedside, compared to families where the mother was the participating parent, so it is plausible that the father’s speech did increase. A robust body of literature in typically developing infants ﬁnds that infants hear signiﬁcantly more speech from mothers than fathers [41, 42]. and this has also been found in the NICU setting [15, 43]. Fathers may be a particularly important source of language input in the NICU, especially if medical conditions limit a mother’s ability to interact. Thus, our ﬁndings suggest that interventions with fathers may be particularly effective at increasing the overall amount of speech infants are exposed to in the NICU. Importantly, the present intervention is highly scalable to other NICU settings. The curriculum consisted of freely available videos and handouts, together taking approximately 30 min to review. Parents generally enjoyed the curriculum and appreciated being provided with actions they could take immediately to support their infants’ development, which is important in settings where parents often feel like they have little control in their child’s outcomes [44]. Given the brevity of the intervention, it could potentially be combined with other language-promoting interventions, such as education to increase parental reading in the

NICU [45, 46]. Future studies of tandem interventions may result in compounded beneﬁts in infant language exposure and subsequent cognitive outcomes. Furthermore, while the intervention was provided individually to families (to preserve the integrity of the intervention/control groups), it could also be offered to multiple families at the same time; this could add the beneﬁt of group support, especially for NICUs with private rooms where families may feel more isolated. Finally, the intervention could potentially be delivered through pre-recorded materials that families can access anytime, though further research is needed to determine if this would have the same efﬁcacy as in-person interactions with a staff member. While the present study is highly encouraging, it does have limitations. First, to determine initial feasibility, the intervention was only provided in English; further research is needed to examine the efﬁcacy of translations of the intervention into other languages, and adaptations for cultures with less attention to child-directed speech. Second, the control was a passive “care as usual” condition, rather than an active control (e.g., an unrelated intervention). Thus, it is possible that intervention effects could be due to factors other than the intervention content (e.g., having a one-on-one discussion with a staff member); however, given the combined changes in both parent knowledge of language development and actual language practices, this is unlikely. Third, the LENA does not distinguish between infant directed speech and non-directed speech, such as nurses and parents talking to each other, or parents talking on the phone. However, since this percentage would not be

expected to consistently increase in the Time 2 compared to Time 1 LENA recording, and only in the intervention group, we do not expect this to alter to our ﬁndings. Fourth, because our study sample was predominantly White, non-Hispanic, and highly educated, it may limit assessment of the intervention’s impacts on parents from minoritized race and ethnicities and with lower educational attainment; however, initial ﬁndings suggest enhanced effects for families with lower education. Finally, while we demonstrate immediate intervention effects similar to those of longer, more intensive interventions, it is important to examine long-term effects on parent language practices and ultimately children’s linguistic and cognitive outcomes. There is a risk of intervention fade out [47]. in which the noted initial new behavior returns to baseline without reinforcement. More studies following knowledge retention and language behavior over a longer course duration are needed before conclusions can be drawn regarding long term effects.

CONCLUSION This study demonstrates the effectiveness of a brief, accessible, feasible educational intervention to improve the quantity and quality of parent-infant interaction in the NICU, with the greatest beneﬁt to infants at highest risk of neurocognitive delay. This intervention simultaneously empowers families to participate in their infant’s neurodevelopment while maximizing the prolonged NICU hospitalization to promote optimal language exposure for high-risk infants.
